title: An Execution‑Oriented Evaluation of Generate→Validate→Simulate→Rollback Pipelines for LLM‑Assisted NetOps: a Confirmatory Study with gpt‑5‑mini
abstract: We preregistered (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing (A) a generation‑only baseline and (C) a generate→validate→simulate→rollback (guarded) pipeline for LLM‑assisted NetOps configuration tasks. Using gpt‑5‑mini on N=160 vendor‑neutral tasks (routing/ACL/NAT), a deterministic simulator produced an operational binary outcome (actionable misconfiguration). Observed counts were: baseline actionable = 0/160; guarded actionable = 0/160. Paired difference = 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed=1729); McNemar exact p = 1.00. The preregistered target (≥30% relative reduction) is unevaluable because of a ceiling effect induced by (i) task calibration and (ii) the preregistered shared_initial_generation design (one candidate / task reused across conditions). We report the frozen design, verified numerical outcomes, artifact pointers (file paths and SHA‑256 hashes from the execution manifest), a concise diagnosis of why the confirmatory hypothesis could not be evaluated, and concrete artifact‑rooted prescriptions for follow‑up confirmatory runs.

sections.introduction: Generative models are proposed to automate NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, change planning) but fluent proposals may be operationally unsafe without deterministic pre‑enactment checks and sandboxed enactment [Khurshid et al., VeriFlow 2012]. Prior work couples generation and verification; however, claims about operational benefit require preregistered, artifacted confirmatory evaluation against an operational adjudicator. We preregistered (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) a paired design testing whether a guarded pipeline (generate→validate→simulate→rollback) reduces actionable misconfigurations by ≥30% relative to generation‑only. Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, artifacted paired run with gpt‑5‑mini on N=160 tasks; (2) exact, hash‑verified numerical outcomes and diagnostic artifacts; (3) an evidence‑based diagnosis explaining why the preregistered contrast was unevaluable in this run; (4) concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for subsequent confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: Verifier‑in‑the‑loop work (VeriFlow) established runtime/insertion invariant checking for SDN [Khurshid et al., SIGCOMM 2012]. Recent NetOps/IBN literature proposes generate‑validate‑repair and constraint guidance (MeshAgent, GraphSynth, MNC, Flow‑of‑Action families) and benchmarks (OpsEval, LogEval) that measure question/answer performance but typically stop short of deterministic enactment adjudication. Our run differs by preregistration, deterministic simulator adjudication, and full archival of prompts, model calls, scorer JSONs, and analysis artifacts to permit independent re‑scoring.
sections.methodology: Preregistration (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1). The preregistration froze: task selection (N=160; cluster targets: routing ≈64, ACL ≈64, NAT/other ≈32); augmentation seeds [42,123,999]; model scope = gpt‑5‑mini; paired design with shared_initial_generation (one candidate generated per task and used in both conditions); maximum model calls = 320; primary estimand = paired difference in actionable misconfiguration proportion (A minus C); analysis plan = paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) and McNemar exact. Execution and artifacts. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter executed the run; all raw outputs, provider logs, canonicalized configurations, scoring JSONs, and analysis artifacts were archived and SHA‑256 hashed in the execution manifest. Key manifest files (SHA‑256): execution/raw_results.jsonl = 2445d0f8e9be9cfa34ede1bbe80b82d6f05b51bcafc7c1688d0ed8e1c73d8044; execution/result_schema.json = 63199db3f7219b969acc5497fae613c8d5df16e081768969f67b7b3024844465; execution/transformation_manifest.json = 28c190a50d06bf19894639f0ed6edc7b2dc3771138bd818422c212c316bf7c5c; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv = fba3b0ca21c7c7c380ed1134b4fce48b0870bf72a7be0fd8610bf7e6b63a970b. Pipeline semantics. Baseline (A): canonicalize the shared generated candidate and score it via the deterministic simulator (binary actionable predicate). Guarded (C): same shared candidate → constraint validator → deterministic simulator → record enacted/blocked decision. The shared_initial_generation policy preserves exact pairing on candidate content; it was preregistered to isolate validator/simulator effects from generation variance but can induce ceiling effects (Methods caveat). Simulator adjudication. The deterministic simulator returns actionable ∈ {true,false} per canonicalized configuration (schema in execution/result_schema.json). Scoring JSONs for each task include the actionable flag and detailed triggers (see execution/scoring/*.json hashes in the manifest).

sections.discussion: Primary interpretation. The preregistered hypothesis (H1: guarded pipeline reduces actionable misconfigurations by ≥30%) is unevaluable in this run because the baseline actionable rate was zero—the shared generated candidate per task was already non‑actionable to the deterministic simulator. Root cause (artifact‑backed): (i) task calibration and the generator prompts produced candidates adjudicated non‑actionable for all confirmatory tasks; and (ii) the preregistered shared_initial_generation policy (one candidate reused for both conditions) prevents the guarded pipeline from demonstrating per‑task improvement when the shared candidate is non‑actionable. Design implications. A shared‑candidate paired design isolates validator/simulator mechanics but risks ceiling effects when candidate quality is high. To detect guarded‑pipeline benefits one of the following changes is necessary: (a) calibrate the confirmatory set to include adversarial/harder instances that yield a nonzero baseline actionable rate (use archived augmentation scripts and seeds); (b) switch to independent per‑condition generation (increase model calls and variance but allow guarded machinery to intercept faulty candidates); or (c) broaden simulator predicates to capture more failure modes. Construct and external validity. Construct validity depends on the simulator predicate—inspect execution/result_schema.json to judge alignment to operational severity. External validity is limited by single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini) and simulator abstraction vs live enactment. Operational recommendation (artifact‑rooted). For a follow‑up confirmatory run executable from the archived scripts: (1) run a discovery collection using the archived augmentation seeds to find tasks with nonzero baseline actionable rates; (2) preregister independent per‑condition generation and a larger model‑call budget; (3) evaluate at least two models/prompts to improve generality; (4) include human adjudication for a sample to validate simulator actionability semantics. All required scripts and seeds are present in the execution/transformation_manifest.json and execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256s above) and may be reused without inventing new data.
sections.conclusion: We report a fully preregistered, hash‑verified paired confirmatory execution comparing generation‑only and generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipelines using gpt‑5‑mini on N=160 NetOps tasks. Observed baseline actionable = 0/160 and guarded actionable = 0/160, paired difference = 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], McNemar p = 1.00). The preregistered ≥30% relative reduction target is unevaluable due to a ceiling effect caused by task calibration and the shared_initial_generation pairing choice. The run's primary value is artifacted evidence showing how confirmatory design choices interact with generator quality and adjudicator semantics. We provide precise, artifact‑rooted prescriptions (discovery adversarial calibration, independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model scope) for future confirmatory experiments. All canonical artifacts and SHA‑256 hashes required to reproduce the analysis are enumerated in the execution manifest (key hashes are cited in Methods).

disclosure_statement:
Mandatory Disclosure Statement (CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track).

Models and orchestration: primary generative model used = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API). Orchestration/adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The exact Master Prompt bundle used to guide the autonomous run is the Master Prompt v1 — Autonomous CNSM 2026 Research Run, and the autonomy lock boundary and topic constraints (Generative AI & LLMs for NetOps; focus on operational reliability/validation/enactability) were set by the human Research Director prior to the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: collaborative pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred and were explicitly excluded from final empirical evidence as required by the track. Autonomy claim: after the autonomy lock, literature review, research‑gap selection, preregistration, prompt generation, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, manuscript drafting, and revision were performed autonomously. No human manually edited the technical manuscript content, numerical results, figures, captions, references, or this Disclosure Statement after the autonomy lock.

Preregistration and frozen design: the run followed preregistration id c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1, which froze the confirmatory paired design, task selection (N=160; augmentation seeds [42,123,999]), shared_initial_generation policy (one generated candidate per task reused across baseline and guarded), model (gpt‑5‑mini), maximum model calls (320), primary estimand, analysis plan (paired bootstrap 10,000, seed=1729 and McNemar exact), retry policy, and stopping rules. No post‑hoc changes that affected confirmatory inference were made.

Artifact availability and integrity: all raw model outputs, provider call logs, canonicalized configurations, per‑task scoring JSONs, deterministic simulator scoring schema, analysis scripts, and the execution manifest are archived and SHA‑256 hashed. Representative authoritative files and their SHA‑256 values (as recorded in the execution manifest) are: execution/raw_results.jsonl = 2445d0f8e9be9cfa34ede1bbe80b82d6f05b51bcafc7c1688d0ed8e1c73d8044; execution/result_schema.json = 63199db3f7219b969acc5497fae613c8d5df16e081768969f67b7b3024844465; execution/transformation_manifest.json = 28c190a50d06bf19894639f0ed6edc7b2dc3771138bd818422c212c316bf7c5c; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv = fba3b0ca21c7c7c380ed1134b4fce48b0870bf72a7be0fd8610bf7e6b63a970b. Per‑task scoring JSONs are under execution/scoring/; their names and hashes are enumerated in the execution manifest. These files constitute the canonical record required to reproduce scoring and the analysis reported herein.

Provider calls and retries: planned maximum model calls = 320; actual provider model calls used = 160 because the preregistered shared_initial_generation design used one generation per task. The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two transient retries for provider errors; none materially affected confirmatory outcomes. The provider call audit in the execution manifest documents these events.

Human role limitations: the Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock development. After autonomy lock, no human performed manual manuscript edits to technical content or numeric results. Some provider operational identifiers are not public for confidentiality, but the prompts, raw outputs, canonicalizers, scoring schema, and per‑file SHA‑256 hashes are archived and enumerated above to support independent re‑scoring given equivalent API access.

Reproducibility instruction (minimal): to reproduce the analysis reported here use the execution manifest file (execution/transformation_manifest.json; SHA‑256 28c190a5...) as the authoritative index, then validate the key archive files (execution/raw_results.jsonl and execution/result_schema.json using the SHA‑256s above) before re‑scoring candidate canonicalizations with the recorded deterministic simulator schema. The analysis scripts and the paired_contingency_table.csv (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 fba3b0ca...) are provided to reproduce the statistical summaries and bootstrap confidence intervals.
limitations: Ceiling effect: the baseline generation produced zero actionable misconfigurations under the chosen deterministic simulator (baseline = 0/160), making the preregistered ≥30% relative‑reduction target unevaluable.

Shared‑candidate policy: the preregistered shared_initial_generation (one candidate per task reused across baseline and guarded) prevents the guarded pipeline from demonstrating benefit on tasks where the shared candidate is already non‑actionable.
Single‑model scope: conclusions apply to gpt‑5‑mini and the exact prompts/call budget used; multi‑model generality is unresolved.

Construct abstraction: the deterministic simulator predicate is an abstraction and may not capture all production failure modes; human adjudication may be required to validate actionability semantics for production claims.
No live device enactment: evaluation used a deterministic simulator rather than live production enactment, limiting external validity to production rollouts.
